guidance.cx-usage-guidance: Use cx-usage-guidance only on a component reference or maintainer surface that displays the canonical guidance text. Set editable to false anywhere the reader must not change framework authority; when editing is allowed, persist textChange through the owning guidance store and surface saving or error state truthfully. Do not place this reference tool in product UI.
guidance.cx-slot-marker: Use cx-slot-marker only in component workbenches and reference examples to make a projected slot visible without inventing realistic product content. Name the actual slot and choose inline or block to match its layout role. It is inspection tooling, not a placeholder, empty state, or product component.
guidance.cx-chat-message: Use cx-chat-message for one authored entry inside cx-chat-thread. Provide stable authorId and author text, let the parent thread compare authorId with viewerId to label the viewer as You, and project the message body. Supply a localized timestamp only when it helps sequence the conversation; use status for genuine message state, not decorative metadata.
guidance.cx-chat-thread: Use cx-chat-thread to group an ordered conversation and its composer or supporting footer. Project cx-chat-message instances into the message list, put the input or thread actions in the footer slot, and provide viewerId so each message can distinguish the viewer from other authors. Do not use it as a generic activity feed or unordered comment container.
guidance.cx-account-control: Use cx-account-control for the signed-in identity and account-level actions in persistent application navigation. Provide the current username and handle logout explicitly; omit menuItems when log out is the only account action, or pass a focused account menu and handle itemSelect. Do not mix page, entity, or navigation actions into the account menu.
guidance.cx-action-bar: Use cx-action-bar only while the selection count is greater than zero. Keep the count truthful, provide Deselect all, and scope every action to the current selection rather than the whole collection. Group closely related actions, reserve priority primary for the main bulk outcome, and keep destructive mood proportional to consequence. Remove the bar as soon as the selection clears by passing no data.
guidance.cx-detail-panel-section: Use cx-detail-panel-section as a direct child of cx-detail-panel to group one coherent set of details on its own panel-owned surface. Keep related label-value rows, evidence, or history together and let the section own its padding and boundary. Do not use it as a standalone card or project unsectioned content into a detail-panel body.
guidance.cx-dynamic-fields: Use cx-dynamic-fields when users may add or remove values from a defined catalog of optional fields. Give every option a stable id and label, keep fields controlled through fields and fieldsChange, and mark genuinely secret values as masked so they use the password field. Do not use it for a fixed form or allow arbitrary field definitions the product cannot interpret.
guidance.cx-state-message: Use cx-state-message when an expected content region is wholly empty, filtered to no results, waiting, completed, scheduled, or unavailable. Choose the state that matches the real cause, keep the heading and description specific, and add primary or secondary actions only when they provide the next useful path. Use the content slot only when the standard copy-and-action structure cannot express the necessary recovery. Each state brings the mark that matches it, so supply icon only to override that mark, and visual to drop it altogether.
guidance.cx-labeled-row: Use cx-labeled-row as the default structure for forms, compact facts, and settings that should scan as one stable label column with the value or control beside it. Choose the content kind that matches the real value, keep comparable rows at the same size, and use optional only when absence is allowed. It stacks the label above the value only when its own container becomes too narrow for a readable horizontal row. Do not use it for long prose, unrelated controls, or content without a label-value relationship.
guidance.cx-navigation-recovery: Use cx-navigation-recovery once at the application root with provideCxNavigationRecovery and cxNavigationRecoveryHandler when lazy routes can fail after a release. Maintain the matching cx-build-id and no-store /cx-build.json contract, let the user choose Retry or Reload, and never reload automatically while work may be unsaved. Keep optional diagnostics same-origin, bounded, and free of queries, form state, and error content.
guidance.cx-null-controller: Use cx-null-controller when a value may intentionally inherit or remain unset until the user enables an explicit override and chooses one option. Keep enabled and selectedId controlled, label the inherited-versus-overridden decision clearly, and provide mutually exclusive options with stable ids. Do not use it for an ordinary on/off preference or when null has no meaningful product state.
guidance.cx-top-bar: Use cx-top-bar as the in-application page header: one clear page title, a compact trailing action cluster, and an entity- or page-level overflow menu when needed. Title it one of two ways through the pageTitle input. A heading title is the default: one page heading with an optional concise description. A breadcrumbs title replaces the heading with a trail and carries no description; reach for it when the page sits inside a hierarchy the reader needs to see and step back through, and note that a single-item trail reads as a smaller heading. Keep primary work visible in the actions slot and secondary utilities in menuItems. Enable editableDescription only when description editing is a real saved product behavior.
guidance.cx-radio-reveal: Use cx-radio-reveal for a small mutually exclusive choice where selecting one defined option may reveal one short supporting text value. Keep selectedId and revealValue controlled, use revealHint to explain the extra value, and preserve it when the owner intends reversible switching. Use ordinary radios when no option reveals input, and use a fuller form when the revealed branch needs multiple controls.
guidance.cx-side-nav:
Use cx-side-nav for the application’s primary, persistent navigation hierarchy. Order destinations by user priority and frequency, write labels with strong information scent, and keep nesting shallow enough to scan. Use groups and badges only when they carry meaningful structure or attention; use cx-index-nav for contextual navigation within one active section.

For every internal destination, including a query-driven view, use routerLink. Add queryParams when the query identifies the view—for example, routerLink: '/prototype' with queryParams: { view: 'scans' }—so the real link, active treatment, and aria-current="page" all describe one destination. In routerLinkActiveOptions, use queryParams: 'exact' when the complete query must match, or queryParams: 'subset' when the parent view should remain active while a detail parameter is present. Use queryParamsHandling only when merge or preserve is genuinely part of the destination.

Pass a typed UrlTree when the consumer has already built the complete destination. Do not combine a UrlTree with queryParams, queryParamsHandling, or fragment; cx-side-nav rejects that incompatible definition. Reserve href for genuinely external destinations, optionally with target and rel, never as a workaround for an internal query-driven route.
guidance.cx-wizard-dialog-step: Use ng-template[cxWizardDialogStep] only inside cx-wizard-dialog to bind one step body to the same stable id used in the presented steps array. Provide one template for every reachable step and keep its content focused on that step’s required decision. The owner derives conditional steps before rendering; the directive does not hide, reorder, or recover missing steps.
guidance.cx-active-workbench: Use cxActiveWorkbench only on reference-workbench templates so the active specimen is instantiated while inactive specimens and their global listeners, observers, and overlays do not exist. Bind it to the reference surface’s active component state. It is lifecycle tooling and must never gate ordinary product content.
guidance.cx-workbench: Use cx-workbench only to inspect a public component API in the component reference. Put the literal specimen in the preview, exact public prop controls in the controls slot, and contextual explanation in cxWorkbenchNote. Keep applicable shared width, height, and alignment controls enabled; do not turn scenarios, visual hacks, or workbench-only values into pretend component props.
guidance.cx-menu-trigger: Use cxMenuTrigger on the single native button, cx-button, or cx-icon-button projected as a cx-menu trigger. Keep it inside the owning menu so focus, open state, keyboard behavior, and accessible relationships stay coordinated. Do not attach it to unsupported hosts, multiple nested buttons, or a control that performs a separate action on the same activation.
guidance.cx-index-nav: Use cx-index-nav as secondary navigation for the contents of one active section, beside rather than instead of the primary side navigation. Group destinations by the user’s mental model, keep item labels and searchText findable, and use the built-in filter when the set is large enough to need it. Allow collapse when content width matters; do not use it for app-wide navigation.
guidance.cx-masthead: Use cx-masthead for brand identity and primary wayfinding on a marketing, portfolio, or other public landing surface. Provide one brand treatment, a focused set of navigation links, and real router or href targets; the component owns narrow-width menu collapse. Use cx-top-bar for application page chrome and cx-side-nav for persistent in-app navigation.
guidance.cx-process: Use cx-process when an ordered lifecycle is also the main quick filter for work moving toward a settled end state. Give each stage a stable id, truthful count, and terminal meaning; let selectedId control the filtered view. All clear is valid only when every non-terminal stage is known to contain zero items. Do not use the rail for unrelated categories or fabricate counts to suggest progress.
guidance.cx-popover-demo: Use cx-popover-demo only in framework reference surfaces to demonstrate anchored popover scenarios, alignment, width constraints, and option behavior. It bundles a trigger and sample content for inspection, so it must not ship as product UI. Products compose cx-popover, cx-menu, or the appropriate higher-level pattern directly.
guidance.cx-process-pill: Use cx-process-pill as the presentational stage unit composed by cx-process, or as a non-interactive status legend with the same lifecycle meaning. Keep count undefined when unknown and use zero only for a known empty stage; mood colors the indicator, while selected, terminal, muted, and dense describe rail state. Do not use it as a general-purpose tag or standalone interactive control.
guidance.cx-password-field: Use cx-password-field for passwords and other secret text that must be masked by default. Set the correct name and autocomplete value, keep constraints in hint text, and show validation beside the field. The reveal control auto-hides after revealSeconds and must remain optional user intent; do not use a generic text field for passwords or use this component for ordinary identifiers and verification codes.
guidance.cx-action-area:
Use cx-action-area only when the product scope explicitly requires one. It is not a normal wrapper or automatic enhancement for content that happens to have actions. When action-area use has not been explicitly required, use ordinary inline actions, the entity menu, section content, or navigation and omit cx-action-area.

When explicitly required, it wraps a complete content block that should own local contextual actions without changing the block's normal layout, such as a summary card, labeled details, a status block, or a compact signal. Use info, askAi, support, and editable for the standard block actions. They render as one right-aligned action group in this order: Info, Ask AI, Support, custom actions, Edit. Use actions only for extra custom actions that belong to the same block.

The outline and action group reveal after a short delay so passing over content does not feel twitchy. The action group should stay on one line. When it no longer fits, it first hides shortcut hints from every button. If it still does not fit, buttons with icons become icon-only buttons and expose the original action text in a tooltip. Keep actions local to the wrapped content. Do not use action area as a page toolbar, a card replacement, or a way to hide primary actions. Shortcuts should only trigger while the area is hovered or focused, and each visible shortcut must actually work in that context.
guidance.cx-alert:
Use alerts for contextual feedback that explains a state the user needs to notice and understand. Do not use them for ordinary descriptive copy, banners, toasts, or field validation. Use mood for semantic intent: default for light emphasis, info for important context, success for confirmation, warning for preventable risk, and danger for failure or a blocked action. Mood colors the heading, leading visual, and action; supporting content and dismiss stay neutral.

Provide a concise heading and project supporting paragraphs, lists, or inline links through the default slot. Set loading while work is in progress; the spinner replaces the mood icon. Leave action and dismissible inactive by default. Add one action only when the alert has a direct next step; it sits below the supporting content rather than at the far edge. Set action.href for navigation; omit it and handle actionSelect for an in-place command. Action and dismiss may coexist. Make an alert dismissible only when the user can safely ignore it after reading.
guidance.cx-badge:
Use badges as compact attention markers attached to controls, navigation items, or avatars. Leave count and text empty for the normal dot. Add count only when the number helps the user act, such as unread notifications, selected items, or active filters; values above 99 display as 99+.

Use text for very short labels such as NEW or BETA. Badge text is visually uppercase and should stay at five characters or fewer. Use a tag when the wording needs more room. Never supply count and text together.

Use default for ordinary attention, accent for novelty, success for completion, warning for caution, and danger for urgent risk. Keep the meaning readable without relying on color, and provide ariaLabel whenever the badge communicates information.
guidance.cx-banner:
Use banners for rare, important, time-sensitive information that needs broad attention at the top of the affected surface. Use quieter inline or page-level feedback when the message does not earn that interruption.

A banner must not cover essential navigation, actions, or page content. Dismissibility controls whether a transient message can be removed; it does not decide whether the layout becomes obstructed. Let users dismiss transient banners. A persistent unresolved state may remain visible, but it needs a direct action, acknowledgement, or clear explanation of why it cannot disappear.

Keep banner copy short, direct, and specific. Include an action only when it is the real next step.
guidance.cx-avatar:
Use avatars to identify a person, account, team, or system at a glance. Prefer an image when it is stable and recognizable. Otherwise, use the name so the initials stay consistent and readable.

Avatars should support recognition, not decoration. Keep the color automatic unless the surrounding product already has a meaningful color choice. Use the badge only as a small attention marker, and let it keep the default badge color so identity and status do not compete.
guidance.cx-breadcrumbs:
Use breadcrumbs when the user is inside a real hierarchy and needs to understand where the current page lives. They are not a replacement for back, and they should not appear on shallow pages just to fill space.

Keep the first and current level visible. When the path is too deep or the space is too narrow, collapse the middle levels into the hidden-level menu. Use switchable crumbs only when the user can stay in the same kind of view while changing a scope, source, customer, or other level in the hierarchy.
guidance.cx-budget:
Use budgets to show how a value relates to a known limit. They work best when the user needs to understand pace, remaining capacity, or whether usage is getting close to a boundary. Use percent when the exact unit is not important, currency when the amount itself changes the decision, and unit for things like seats, credits, hours, or storage. Use unitLabel for the text shown after counted values, such as seats, credits, hours, or GB.

Use the compact variant when the budget is a small supporting signal. Use the detailed variant when both the current value and the total need to be visible. Favor describes what good looks like: low when a smaller value is better, high when a larger value is better. Add a hint only when the extra context helps the user act, such as expiry, renewal, or reserved budget.
guidance.cx-button:
Use the default button for almost every action. When in doubt, use default. Primary is only for the action that moves the user toward their goal, and it should usually appear once per view or once inside the element it belongs to.

Set href when the control navigates so it renders as a semantic anchor; omit href for commands. Use danger for destructive actions, and make the surrounding flow add enough friction before something is lost. Use transparent when the action should stay quiet inside dense UI, toolbars, menus, or supporting controls. Use rounded only when a pill shape is intentional. Button text should name the action, not the state: "Delete file" beats "Confirm". Use shortcutParts only to display a shortcut that is handled by the surrounding context; the button itself does not own keyboard shortcut behavior. Icon-only buttons need a clear ariaLabel.
guidance.cx-card:
Use cards to group one self-contained piece of content. The default card uses a 4px surface-alt frame, with the header sitting directly on that frame and the content inside a rounded surface island.

Add border when a repeated card needs a clearer object edge, such as dense boards; bordered cards use the 1px line instead of the 4px frame. Add shadow when the card needs a little lift from the canvas without changing its structure. Add a header when the card needs a title, icon, status, local menu, or meta content. Use the meta slot for small supporting status such as a tag. Use menuItems only for actions that belong to that card.

A whole-card target navigates or acts, never both. Set href when it opens another location so the card exposes a real link and does not emit pressed. Set interactive only for an in-place action that emits pressed, so it exposes a real button. Combining both modes warns and href wins. The menu stays a separate sibling control in either mode. Do not put additional links, buttons, or fields in an activatable card body; use the card menu or leave the card passive. Use padding="none" only when the content needs to sit flush, such as tables, charts, media, or custom layouts. Use padding="large" when a card needs a roomier 16px rhythm inside the header and content island.

Set expandable when a card holds more content than a scanning surface such as a dashboard should show at rest. Collapsed, the content clamps to previewHeight (default 240px) behind a fade, and a full-width chevron control at the card's foot toggles it between the preview and its natural height, announcing Show more or Show less to assistive tech. The control is earned by overflow: content that fits renders a completely normal card, so expandable is safe to leave on for content of varying length. Keyboard focus moving into the clipped region expands the card automatically. Do not combine expandable with href or interactive; a whole-card link or action cannot host an inner control, and the card reports a console error and ignores expandable.

Use tabs when one card holds a few peer views of the same subject, such as two related comment threads. Pass tabs and selectedTabId and switch the projected content on selectedTabIdChange; the card renders the tab row as a dedicated flush section between the header and the content island, and the content region becomes the tab panel. Tabs placed inside the content keep the normal padded treatment; the dedicated section is only for the top position. Do not combine tabs with href or interactive; the card reports a console error and ignores tabs. Tabs compose with expandable: the tab row stays visible and only the content clamps, re-measuring per tab.
guidance.cx-code-field:
Use code fields only for short one-time verification codes. They are for moments where the user is copying a six-character code from email, SMS, an authenticator app, or a recovery flow.

Do not use a code field for passwords, serial numbers, IDs, invite codes, API keys, or long tokens. Passwords need password fields. Other long values need normal text fields because the user may need to read, select, edit, or paste the value as one piece. Keep validation close to the field, and let paste work generously.
guidance.cx-split-button:
Use split buttons only when one action has a clear default and the menu contains close variations of that same action. The main side runs the default action; the chevron opens related alternatives.

Do not use a split button for unrelated actions or as a way to hide decisions the user must make first. If there is no obvious default action, use a menu button instead. Keep labels direct, keep destructive alternatives visibly dangerous, and use primary only when the default action is the main path forward.
guidance.cx-variant:
Use variants to show realistic examples of how a component can be used. Each tab should represent a meaningful scenario, state, or composition that helps someone understand the component in context, not just a prop value in isolation.

Variants are not a full workbench and should not try to expose every prop. Use them when the useful question is "what does this look like in real product use?" Keep the names short, choose examples people would actually build, and let the specimen do the explaining.
guidance.cx-big-checkbox:
Use a big checkbox when one binary choice needs more room than a small checkbox can give it. It works well for permissions, setup choices, and options where the label needs a short explanation.

The state is only selected or not selected. The optional icon sits on the far right as a 24px square-subtle icon. Use iconMood only to color that icon treatment; it should not change the checkbox surface. Use the content slot below the text for small supporting content that belongs inside the option, such as metadata or a compact preview. Keep the copy short and make the whole item easy to scan. If the choice is part of a long form or a dense table, use a regular checkbox instead.
guidance.cx-big-radio:
Use a big radio when the user must choose one clear option from a small set. It is best for choices that need a title, a short explanation, or a more touch-friendly target.

The optional icon sits on the far right as a 24px square-subtle icon. Use iconMood only to color that icon treatment; it should not change the radio surface. Use the content slot below the text for small supporting content that belongs inside the option, such as metadata or a compact progress signal. Keep the options parallel so they are easy to compare. If the choice is simple and space is tight, use regular radios instead.
guidance.cx-button-group:
Use a button group for a small set of closely related choices where one choice is active at a time. It should feel faster than a dropdown and clearer than several separate buttons.

Set ariaLabel to the dimension being chosen, such as View or Sort order, so the options have one specific group name. Keep option labels short and make each option the same kind of decision. Disabled choices are skipped by the tab stop and every navigation key; never leave focus trapped on an unavailable choice. If there are many options or the labels become long, use a dropdown instead.
guidance.cx-calendar:
Use a calendar when the date itself matters in relation to nearby days. It is useful for planning, scheduling, and choosing dates where weekday context helps. Date picker and date span picker use the same calendar so month navigation, constraints, focus, and selection stay consistent.

Use single selection for one date and range selection for a start and end date. Use embedded only inside another floating surface. Do not use a calendar when the user only needs to enter a known date quickly. In that case, a date field is quieter and faster.
guidance.cx-chart:
Use charts to show shape, trend, comparison, or proportion. A chart should answer a real question faster than a table would.

Keep the chart focused. If the user needs exact values, pair it with a table or use a simpler metric instead.
guidance.cx-column-filter-editor:
Use a column filter editor when one column needs the same filtering interaction in a table header and a shared filter surface. Choose search for text, multi-select for named choices, tag-field for tagged choices, and date-span for a start and end. Multi-select choices render as an inline checklist so users never have to open a second popover; its Clear action appears only after a choice is selected. Keep the value controlled and JSON-safe; empty values resolve to undefined.

Use queryChange and loadMore for remotely filtered or paged multi-select options. The tag-field kind is selection-only and never creates tags. Reuse one definition and value wherever the same column filter appears instead of building a second filter UI.
guidance.cx-checkbox:
Use a checkbox for an independent on/off choice. It should describe a state that can be true or false without changing the meaning of nearby controls.

Write the label as the thing being enabled. Avoid negative labels, because they make checked and unchecked states harder to reason about.
guidance.cx-code-block:
Use a code block when the user needs to read or copy code, commands, logs, or structured text. It should preserve spacing and make the content feel separate from body copy.

Keep surrounding explanation short. If the code is only a tiny value, use inline code or a snippet instead.
guidance.cx-color-picker:
Use a color picker when choosing a raw palette hue is the actual task. It is useful for labels, charts, and visual customization where the color itself is the choice.

Do not use semantic moods such as success, warning, danger, primary, or accent as selectable colors. Those belong in mood props. Keep free color choice rare in product UI.
guidance.cx-context-dialog:
Use a context dialog for a small decision that belongs to the thing the user just interacted with. It should feel local, quick, and specific. When it is the topmost visible, active overlay, Escape follows the same Cancel path as its visible Cancel button. Without that action it still consumes Escape so a parent overlay cannot react. After the parent removes it and surviving-surface focus maintenance settles, the exact connected, visible, and focusable invoker is the final focus target unless a newer top overlay opened. An invalid invoker falls back to the established target inside its owning surviving parent surface.

Do not use it for heavy workflows or important confirmations. If the decision affects the whole page or needs more space, use a dialog.
guidance.cx-date-picker:
Use a date picker when the user needs one specific date. It should make choosing a nearby date easy while still allowing direct entry when the date is known.

Keep helper text close to the field only when it prevents mistakes. Do not add extra explanation for obvious dates. If empty, the picker placeholder should read like Select date unless a selected value is already present.
guidance.cx-date-span-picker:
Use a date span picker when the user needs a start and end date that belong together. It is best for reports, filters, bookings, and time windows.

Make the selected range easy to understand at a glance. If the range has limits or consequences, say that before the user commits. If empty, the picker placeholder should read like Select date range unless a selected value is already present.
guidance.cx-dialog:
Use a dialog when the user must make a focused decision without losing the current page. It should be reserved for important choices, short forms, or confirmations that need attention. Confirm dialogs map Escape to the same Cancel path as the secondary button and Mod+Enter to the primary action; info dialogs map Mod+Enter to Close, and dismissible info dialogs map Escape to the same Dismiss path as their close button. Only the topmost visible, active overlay owns Escape, and later-opened overlays paint above their parents regardless of template order. A non-dismissible top dialog still consumes the key without closing, nested overlays dismiss one at a time, and one keypress emits at most one action. Their shortcut hints sit outside the buttons and appear after the footer has been hovered for one second.

While open, the dialog owns focus. It chooses an enabled action or projected control first, falls back to the dialog surface when nothing is available, and contains both Tab directions through dynamic loading and action changes. After close teardown and surviving-parent focus maintenance settle, the exact connected, visible, and focusable invoker is the final focus target unless a newer top overlay opened. An invalid invoker falls back to the established heading or surface inside its owning surviving parent, never the document body, removed content, or behind another active modal. Consumers do not add local focus handlers or artificial tab stops.

Keep the dialog small and purposeful. If the content grows into a workflow, it probably belongs on its own page or in a fullscreen dialog. Outside clicks should not dismiss a dialog by default. Enable dismissOnClickOutside only for low-consequence dialogs where accidental closure cannot lose work. Supply menuItems only when the dialog needs secondary actions that belong to its current task; an empty or omitted collection leaves the header menu out. Projected body content always sits inside the dialog's padded, scrollable content region, and the description paragraph appears only when description is set, so consumers never add their own dialog padding or scroll container.
guidance.cx-detail-panel:
Use a detail panel as a deeper view of one entity without losing the surrounding collection. Preserve the entity’s identity, state, and already-visible facts before adding detail. The body must then provide a meaningful breakdown beyond the source summary: add the relevant context, evidence, timing, relationships, and history needed to understand the entity and its main state. Do not stop at a restyled summary, let an action area substitute for detail, or invent unavailable information. The panel fills the entire available application frame beneath any explicit persistent utility bar; its source table, card, split pane, or other content region never determines its height. Floating covers the canvas without changing its geometry. Fixed stays attached to the frame edge while the owning application body reserves the panel’s rendered width, reflowing only that body beside it. Below the mobile breakpoint, both variants fill the available application frame and fixed reserves no space.

Keep the header order identity, the entity’s main status, then the rightmost entity overflow menu. When an entity has a main status, project exactly one cx-status-tag through detail-panel-status at the right of the header immediately before the menu. Never substitute severity, classification, or secondary metadata for the main status, and never repeat it in the body, tabs, or footer. Leave detail-panel-status empty rather than inventing a status for an entity without one. Open details through source activation rather than an action-menu command. Use the same menuItems collection and menuItemSelect handler for the table-row kebab, right-click menu, other source menu, and detail-panel kebab; they must match exactly in action set, order, availability, disabled state, and danger treatment. Never copy actions into a panel-only model or handler. Leave menuItems empty only when the entity has no action menu anywhere; provide menuAriaLabel only when its heading-derived label is not specific enough.

The panel uses a quiet grey frame behind separate white surfaces. When tabs are supplied, they sit immediately beneath the header, transparent, undivided, and without surrounding padding or a rounded island. The body scrolls vertically only. Content that genuinely requires horizontal movement, such as a wide table, owns its own bounded scroller. Present compact label-value facts as horizontal labeled rows by default, with labels in one stable leading column and values beside them. Use a vertical label-value layout only when the product explicitly requires it or a documented narrow-layout constraint makes the horizontal row unreadable. Keep the orientation consistent across comparable detail surfaces. Wrap each content group in cx-detail-panel-section; every section supplies a white surface, discreet border, fixed 16px padding, and an 8px gap between direct children. Do not project unsectioned body content, remove section padding, or recreate this structure in page styles. Use selectedTabId for controlled tab selection.

The close button is the only footer control by default. The main status belongs only in the header; supporting metadata, navigation, and passive copy belong in content, while ordinary entity actions belong in the shared entity menu. A pinned panel-wide task may add persistent completion controls only when they must remain reachable while its body scrolls. The panel remains dismissible through its close button and Escape. Keep child overlays layered: a menu, picker, popover, or dialog opened from the panel closes before the panel responds to Escape or outside interaction. Enable dismissOnClickOutside only when losing the panel is safe. Do not guard dismissal with selectors.
guidance.cx-divider:
Use a divider to separate groups that need a visible pause. It should help the eye understand structure, not decorate the page.

If spacing alone is enough, skip the divider. Too many lines make an interface feel heavier than it is.
guidance.cx-validation-message:
Use a validation message to explain state or recovery near the field or action it belongs to. Preserve its meaning in every presentation: status stays neutral, info stays informational, success confirms, warning warns, and error blocks or fails. Global presentation must not turn them all into danger.

Write it in plain language. Do not blame the user, and do not show validation before the user has had a fair chance to act.
guidance.cx-expansion-panel:
Use an expansion panel for secondary information that is useful but not always needed. It helps keep the page calm while still making details easy to reach.

The heading must clearly promise what will open. Avoid hiding critical information inside a collapsed panel.
guidance.cx-drop-zone:
Use a drop zone when choosing one file is the primary action and a spacious drag target earns its place. The empty state accepts a dropped file or opens the native picker. Once selected, it becomes a compact file row with clear replace and remove actions. Configure accept and maxSize when constraints are known so they appear before selection and rejected files receive specific recovery guidance.

Treat value as controlled and keep lifecycle state tied to the file. A new or replacement file emits selected; the consumer moves that value to uploading, complete, or failed only when it has real evidence. Supply progress only when completion is measured from 0 to 100; omit it for indeterminate uploading. A failed value keeps the file available for Try again, replacement, or removal, and retry emits the retained file without inventing the next state.

Use readonly to present a file and its lifecycle without any interaction. Use disabled when the control is temporarily unavailable. A rejected type or size never displaces the current file. Removing emits null; when a completed value represents a persisted asset, only treat that clear as unlinking or deletion when the surrounding product deliberately owns that consequence.
guidance.cx-file-upload:
Use file upload when the user is adding a file as part of a task. The control should make accepted file types, limits, and current file state easy to understand.

Use the button variant inline in a form when the file is one field among others. Use the zone variant when uploading is the primary action of the surface and the extra room to drag, browse, and preview a list of files earns its place. Both variants accept the same accept, maxSize, and multiple limits, and both surface a rejected file with a specific reason.

Keep one selected-files model from input through output: always pass and read the files array. Single mode limits it to zero or one item; multiple mode may contain several. Do not maintain separate file, hasFile, or fileName state. Show the selected files, upload progress, or the next required action.
guidance.cx-filter-bar:
Use a filter bar when a table needs a coordinated collection toolbar for relevant filters, query mode, saved views, and display properties. Do not use the whole pattern when the collection is faster to scan without controls or when its fixed Table properties surface would contain only one meaningful setting; expose that setting directly instead. Supply one filter definition per column and keep filterValues controlled by stable column ids. Under the filter button, make columns searchable and reveal their shared editor in a one-at-a-time accordion. Keep active filters clearable from the collapsed row, show the active count, and retain Clear all for recovery. Pressing an active filter reopens that filter in the same editor the accordion and the column header use, so one filter is adjusted the same way wherever the user reaches it.

Do not give the filter bar a separate filter model from the table it controls. Quick filters are view-scoping shortcuts: selecting one changes which rows are presented, never the entities represented by those rows. The owner applies filtering, sorting, grouping, and saved views to collection or view state, then passes the resulting rows back. Keep Table properties to a relevant, coherent family drawn from display density, grouping, sorting, column visibility, and pinning rather than an arbitrary catch-all.
guidance.cx-item-card:
Use an item card for a row that pairs a labelled thing with one action, such as a settings toggle, a connected device, or a linked account. The icon and heading identify the item; the trailing slot holds a single control.

Keep the trailing control to one clear action. If a row needs several actions or rich content, use a full card or a detail view instead.
guidance.cx-kpi:
Use a KPI to lead with one number that matters and just enough context to make it meaningful: a trend, a target, or a short comparison. It belongs on dashboards and summaries, not inside dense tables.

Show only the context that changes a decision. Too many trends, bars, and footnotes turn a headline metric back into noise.
guidance.cx-rating:
Use a rating to capture or show a score on a small fixed scale. It is interactive by default; set readonly to display an average, including half values.

Keep the scale small and consistent across the product. If exact precision matters more than a quick impression, a number field or slider may be clearer.
guidance.cx-reaction:
Use a reaction to let someone respond to content with a familiar icon and see how many others did the same. The selected state marks the viewer's own reaction.

Choose an icon whose meaning is immediately recognizable, such as thumbs-up or heart. Keep reactions lightweight and optional. If a response needs words or a real decision, use a comment or a named action instead.
guidance.cx-text-shimmer:
Use a text shimmer for a short label that signals active work — generating, thinking, or streaming. The label stays continuously readable while a narrow highlight travels across it; reduced-motion removes the highlight.

Show it only while something is genuinely happening, and keep the label short. For measurable work, a progress bar tells the user more.
guidance.cx-fullscreen-dialog:
Use a fullscreen dialog when a focused task needs a large temporary canvas but should still read as a dialog, not a route change. It uses the standard dialog overlay behind it, opens with space on the top and sides, and keeps rounded top corners so the app context remains perceptible.

The shell does not invent a heading, description, footer, or action buttons. Put a complete visible experience in the content slot, including any local navigation, save, or cancel controls the task needs. Use closeButton only when a close affordance is appropriate; it sits in the overlay's top-right corner outside the canvas.
guidance.cx-grid:
Use a grid when items need to line up in columns and respond cleanly to available space. It is best for cards, metrics, and repeated content blocks.

The grid should serve the content, not force it. If the items need to be read in a strict order, a list may be clearer.
guidance.cx-masonry:
Use masonry for browsing collections whose items have naturally different heights — note walls, image boards, mixed cards. Items keep their own height and pack into columns without uniform row gaps.

Reading order flows down each column, not across rows, so masonry suits scanning over strict sequence. If order matters or the items share one height, use the grid instead.
guidance.cx-icon:
Use icons to support recognition, status, or compact actions. An icon should clarify the interface, not replace words when the meaning could be unclear.

Keep icon use consistent. If an icon needs explanation every time, it probably needs text or a tooltip.
guidance.cx-icon-button:
Use an icon button for compact actions where the icon is already familiar or the space is constrained. It is best for repeated tools and secondary actions.

Always make the accessible name specific. Use rounded when the button should read as a circular control, such as floating or overlay chrome. If the action is important or unfamiliar, use a text button instead.
guidance.cx-image:
Use an image when the user benefits from seeing the actual thing. It should support recognition, inspection, or context.

Avoid decorative images in product UI unless they clearly improve comprehension. Empty or broken image states should still feel intentional.
guidance.cx-inline:
Use inline layout for a small row of related items. It keeps actions, labels, and small metadata aligned without creating a new visual block.

Do not use it for content that needs to wrap into paragraphs or compare across rows. When the row gets crowded, move to a stack or grid.
guidance.cx-text-field:
Use a text field for short free text. The label should name the value the user is entering, and the field should stay close to its label.

Do not use placeholders. Put examples, constraints, and format help in hint text. Do not use it for long notes, rich text, or values with strict formats unless the formatting help is clear.
guidance.cx-email-field:
Use an email field when the user is entering an email address. It owns the label, name, accessibility label, native email keyboard, browser autofill, and email-specific format expectation.

Do not use a generic text field for email addresses. Do not configure the browser plumbing locally. Do not use placeholders. Put examples, domain rules, or restrictions in hint text, and show validation directly beneath the field.
guidance.cx-phone-field:
Use a phone field when the user is entering a phone number and country code matters. It owns the label, input names, accessibility labels, autocomplete behavior, and country-code selector so products do not rebuild that pattern locally.

Do not split the country code into a separate nearby dropdown. Do not use it for numeric identifiers. Be forgiving about spaces and local phone-number formatting.
guidance.cx-lightbox:
Use a lightbox when the user needs to inspect one image or a small ordered gallery without leaving the current page. Provide useful alt text for every image and add captions only when they help explain what is being inspected.

The lightbox closes with Escape or by pressing the surrounding backdrop. Multiple images add finite previous and next controls, Left and Right keyboard navigation, and a visible position cue; do not build competing gallery controls around it. If the media needs editing, comparison, thumbnails, or a longer workflow, use a dedicated view instead.
guidance.cx-list:
Use a list for rows you compose yourself: a row can sit there as information, act when pressed, or open to reveal more. It is the one list primitive, so reach for it whether you are showing a read-only set of facts, a set of things to pick from, or a set of things to open.

Disclosure is an accordion: opening a row closes the previous one, so the user is never comparing two open rows or scrolling past a wall of expanded detail. If a disclosure is one self-contained region rather than a member of a list, or several regions genuinely need to stay open together, use cx-expansion-panel instead.

Keep expandedId controlled when the open row must survive navigation or reload; leave it unset and the list still opens one row at a time on its own. Use flat when the list already sits inside a framed surface such as a card or panel, so the boundary is drawn once.
guidance.cx-list-item:
Use a list item as one row inside cx-list. Give it a heading that reads on its own, and put the value the user is scanning for in meta so the eye can run down the right edge.

A row opens, navigates, or acts, never more than one. Set expandable when pressing the row should reveal its projected content. Set href when it opens another location, so the row body is a real link. Set interactive only for an in-place action that emits pressed, so the row body is a real button. Leave all three unset for a row that is purely information, so it carries no false affordance.

The row must be readable closed. If the user has to open it to find out whether it is the one they want, the heading, description, or meta is doing too little. Put row-level controls in the actions slot; they sit beside the row body rather than inside it, so they stay reachable without triggering the row.
guidance.cx-skeleton-loader:
Use a skeleton loader when content is coming and you already know the shape it will take. It holds that shape with placeholder blocks so the page does not jump when the real content lands, and it tells the user the system is working.

Match the placeholder to the incoming content — table, list, chart, or blocks — and keep the counts close to what will actually arrive; a skeleton that promises six rows and delivers one is a small lie about the wait. Do not use it to cover a slow or unclear state that deserves an explanation, and do not leave it running as a permanent stand-in for content that failed to load.

For a small control or region that is simply busy, a spinner is enough. When the user must stop and wait for the work to finish, use cx-loading-overlay.
guidance.cx-loading-overlay:
Use a loading overlay when the user genuinely cannot continue until indeterminate work finishes, and seeing the work happen is worth taking over the screen. It puts a scrim over the page and shows a spinner with the live status of the work underneath.

Set status to the stage the work is in right now, and set it again each time the work genuinely moves on. Drive it from real progress events; never advance it on a timer or cycle a scripted list of stages, because named stages imply real position in real work and invented ones lie about how far along the user is. Keep each status to a few words. The overlay holds every status on screen long enough to read, so bursts of fast events do not flicker, and it shows only the current stage rather than a history.

It cannot be dismissed: there is no close control, Escape does nothing, and the backdrop ignores clicks. Close it by setting open to false when the work actually finishes, and never leave it open on a path that can fail silently — the user has no way out. If the wait needs a heading, an explanation, or a way out such as cancel, it is a different surface: use cx-dialog. If the user could reasonably keep working, do not take the screen at all; use cx-skeleton-loader to hold the shape of incoming content, or place progress where the result will appear so nothing shifts when it lands.
guidance.cx-log:
Use a log to show a sequence of system events or process steps. It should help the user understand what happened and what may need attention. Build its one complete log model with CxLog.of(entries); each entry owns its step and any timestamp, description, or author, while the log derives connector positions from the final sequence.

Keep entries short and ordered. If the user needs to act on an entry, make the action easy to find.
guidance.cx-log-step:
Use a log step for one item in a process history. The status, label, and time should quickly explain where the process stands.

Do not overload each step with prose. A log is for scanning first, detail second.

Give a step a link with withLink when its text names something that has its own destination: a routerLink for a page in this product, or an href for a system outside it. The text keeps the colour of an unlinked step and gains an underline, so a linked step reads as a log entry rather than a button. Leave it unlinked when the destination would only repeat what the step already says.
guidance.cx-markdown:
Use markdown rendering for trusted, formatted content that needs simple structure. It is useful for notes, guidance, and generated summaries. Article markdown centres its reading measure on an open canvas; set align to start when the article is embedded beside navigation or another fixed column and needs to share the adjacent content edge.

Keep markdown restrained in product UI. Too many heading levels, links, or styles can make the page feel unmanaged.
guidance.cx-markdown-editor:
Use the markdown editor when someone writes formatted text as content — notes, journals, long-form fields. The value stays plain markdown, but the writer sees the formatted result: typing markdown syntax formats in place, and Backspace right after a conversion restores the literal characters.

There is no toolbar and no preview pane on purpose; the writing surface is the preview. Pair it with a debounced saver rather than a save button so writing feels like a normal editor. For raw markdown source editing or annotated technical text, use the text area instead.
guidance.cx-menu:
Use a menu for a short list of contextual actions or compact choices. It should appear where the actions belong, and it must declare whether it is trigger, inline, or context presentation. A trigger presentation uses one real button marked cxMenuTrigger; context presentation opens at the invocation point without activating the object beneath it.

Do not use a menu to hide primary actions. If something is the main next step, keep it visible. Flat items are actions unless type is choice. A group with selection makes its leaf items choices unless an item explicitly declares type action. Actions never acquire choice state or change currentId. Single choices close and update currentId; multiple choices stay open while the owner updates selected state.
guidance.cx-metric:
Use a metric for one important number and its label. It should help the user understand status quickly.

Do not pack too many metrics together. A metric loses power when everything on the page is shouting.
guidance.cx-option:
Use an option for one selectable item inside a choice list. The label should make the choice understandable without extra context.

Use supporting text only when it helps compare options. Keep descriptions close to the label so the row reads as one choice, not two distant columns. Use mood only for semantic signal: danger for destructive actions, success for positive state, warning for caution, info for neutral information, and primary or accent only when the row genuinely needs that emphasis. Use shortcutParts or appendIcon for trailing metadata/actions that truly belong at the far edge. Avoid repeating the same words across every option. Use active for the current navigation target, such as the row reached by arrow keys. Use selected for the committed value. Keep selectedHighlight on when the whole row should read as selected; turn it off when another control, such as a checkbox, already carries the selection state.
guidance.cx-option-group:
Use an option group when related choices need a shared label or small count. It should create structure quietly through spacing and subdued text, not through boxed chrome, dividers, or heavy headings.

Keep groups meaningful. If the grouping does not change how the user decides, it adds friction.

The same row does two jobs. As a group it is a quiet divider between options and stays subdued. As a heading it names a whole surface and reads as its title, so it takes full ink and weight. Choose by what the row is above, not by how much attention it should get.
guidance.cx-pagination:
Use pagination when there are more items than should be shown at once and the user benefits from stable pages. It works well for lists that are browsed or revisited.

Do not paginate tiny lists. If the user is likely to search or filter instead, make those controls strong.
guidance.cx-number-field:
Use a number field when the user must enter an exact numeric value. It should make units, limits, and invalid values clear.

Do not use placeholders. Put examples, constraints, units, and ranges in hint text. Use a slider only when approximate adjustment is the main task. Exact values belong in a number field.
guidance.cx-placeholder:
Use a placeholder to reserve space for content that is missing, loading, or not configured yet. It should explain the empty state without feeling broken.

Do not use placeholders as decoration. They should either help the user wait, understand, or act.
guidance.cx-progress-bar:
Use a progress bar when completion has a clear start and end. Give it a visible label or ariaLabel that names what is progressing, and associate any useful hint. A progress indicator is passive information, never a disabled control.

Avoid fake precision. If progress cannot be measured honestly, use indeterminate progress or a loader instead. Reduced motion keeps indeterminate progress still rather than merely slowing an endless sweep.
guidance.cx-qr-code:
Use a QR code when scanning is genuinely faster than typing or copying. It is useful for device pairing, login handoff, and sharing links across devices.

The component keeps dark modules on a light quiet-zone surface in every theme because those colors belong to the scannable artifact. Do not recolor or invert it. Always provide a fallback. A QR code should never be the only way to complete an important task.
guidance.cx-query-element:
Use a query element to present one readable part of a structured condition. The query field composes grouped field, operator, and value parts into complete clauses.

Keep labels in user language. Consumers should not assemble query logic from visual elements or expose implementation terms to the user.
guidance.cx-query-field:
Use a query field when the user needs to build, inspect, and edit SQL-style conditions in one text-field surface. Supply fields with compatible operators and typed value sources; the component guides field → operator → value, then asks for an explicit AND or OR before another condition. Done appears once the expression can end, and Mod+Enter finishes without opening another connector. In multiple-value lists, Enter toggles the active value; Space does the same while search text is empty. When an unchanged editor is empty, Left and Right move the ink caret across committed query parts while the matching autocomplete follows it. Up and Down move through the current options, Enter applies the active option, and Backspace removes the condition owning the caret; unfinished or dirty edits stay in place so work is never discarded. Persistent per-clause remove buttons are intentionally omitted, while the edit popover keeps a contextual Remove filter action for pointer and touch use.

Keep growVertically on when the full query should remain visible. Set it to false in compact toolbars or dense table headers where one fixed row and horizontal scrolling protect the surrounding layout. Use manual value filtering for remote option sets and keep loading or failure local to that value source. The value is flat: consumers must apply their documented SQL precedence when AND and OR are mixed. Do not use a query field for simple text search, and add parentheses only when grouped logic becomes a real product requirement.
guidance.cx-radio:
Use radios when the user must choose exactly one option from a small set. All options should be visible so the user can compare them.

Avoid using radios for many items or very long labels. A dropdown or searchable control will be easier to scan.
guidance.cx-dropdown:
Use a dropdown for choosing from a larger or less frequently changed set. It keeps the page calm when showing all options would be too much.

Use clear labels and either a selected default or a placeholder shaped as Select [thing], such as Select entity or Select language. Use Select only when no clearer object fits. Required is the default; set optional only when the field is not required. Turn on searchable when the list is long or scanning would slow the user down. All internal copy is customized through translations: Optional, search, clear, loading, no-results heading and support copy, no-options copy, the create action label, and selected-count text. The "No results" heading and no-options fallback stay automatic unless overridden there. Use selection="multiple" when users can choose more than one option. Use creatable only when adding a missing option is a real next step; keep the create action pinned as the footer and let the parent open the creation dialog. For server-filtered or paged lists, use filterMode="manual" with queryChange, hasMore, loadingMore, and loadMore. If users need to compare a small set side by side, radios or a button group may be better.
guidance.cx-secret-display:
Use secret display for sensitive values that must be revealed, copied, or inspected with care. The default state should protect the value.

Make reveal and copy actions deliberate. Do not expose secrets just because there is enough space.
guidance.cx-search-field:
Use a search field when the user is narrowing a collection by typing. It should be easy to find, quick to clear, and forgiving of partial input.

Do not use placeholders. Use a visible label or nearby visible context to name what is being searched; ariaLabel supports accessibility but does not replace that visible purpose. Pair search with good empty states. A no-results state should help the user adjust, not leave them stuck.
guidance.cx-popover:
Use a popover for small supporting content or controls that belong to a trigger. It should be quick to open and quick to leave.

Sizing follows one contract: the content decides the width, the trigger sets the floor, and the viewport sets the ceiling. By default the surface grows to fit its content up to a compact cap so it reads as a local overlay, not a panel. Anchored surfaces pass minWidth so the popover never reads narrower than its trigger, and maxWidth when their content earns a wider cap. Reserve width for genuinely fixed layouts such as calendars. A popover names itself with a heading, which reads as the surface's title and carries the row that trailing content such as a link is projected into; without a heading there is no row. Popover content always sits in at least one soft island. Use multiple islands to create menu dividers instead of drawing divider lines. The surface itself carries no mood; tone comes from the content inside, such as a danger option row. Do not put long workflows in a popover. If the user needs to think, compare, or save work, use a larger surface.
guidance.cx-severity-tag:
Use a severity tag to show how serious something is. It helps users spot risk, urgency, or impact quickly.

Use severity sparingly and consistently. If everything is severe, nothing is.
guidance.cx-shortcut-key:
Use shortcut keys to show keyboard commands in a compact, recognizable way. They are helpful near menus, toolbars, and command references.

Only show shortcuts that actually work in that context. Wrong shortcut hints erode trust fast.
guidance.cx-slider:
Use a slider when the user is choosing a value by feel within a known range. It works best for approximate settings such as intensity, size, or volume.

Do not use a slider when the exact number matters. Give the user a number field or another exact control instead.
guidance.cx-snippet:
Use a snippet for short copyable text such as tokens, paths, commands, or IDs. It should make copying easier without turning the page into a code block.

Keep the snippet compact and readable. If the content wraps heavily, use a code block instead.
guidance.cx-spinner:
Use a spinner for very small loading states where preserving layout is not important. It should signal that a single control or small area is busy.

Avoid using spinners as the main page state. Larger waits need clearer feedback.
guidance.cx-split:
Use split layout when two areas need to sit beside each other with a clear relationship. It is useful for master-detail, summary-detail, and preview-edit patterns.

Keep the relationship obvious. If the two sides are unrelated, use separate sections instead.
guidance.cx-stack:
Use stack layout when content should flow vertically with consistent rhythm. It is the default way to group horizontal form rows, settings sections, and other grouped content; it does not change the label-and-control orientation inside a form row.

Let the stack carry spacing instead of adding one-off margins. This keeps pages easier to maintain.
guidance.cx-sso-button:
Use an SSO button for signing in with a trusted provider. The provider name should be clear and the button should not look like a generic action.

Only show providers that are actually available. Authentication choices should feel reliable, not experimental.
guidance.cx-status-tag:
Use a status tag to show the current state of an item or process. It should help users scan lists and understand what needs attention.

Keep statuses stable and plain. Avoid clever labels that make state harder to interpret.
guidance.cx-switch:
Use a switch for a setting that takes effect as on or off. It is best for preferences, visibility, and feature toggles.

Use a checkbox instead when the choice is part of a form submission or the user is selecting items from a list.
guidance.cx-table:
Use a table when users need to compare rows and columns. It should make scanning, sorting, filtering, and finding patterns easier than cards or freeform layout would.

Put the most important columns first and keep cell content concise. When a heading or value is clipped, the table uses the shared cxTooltip overflow treatment to reveal the same complete DOM text without adding a tab stop to every cell; task-critical content must remain visible. Never add a native title tooltip to a cell or header. Give a column a filter definition only when narrowing that value is useful; its header menu renders the matching search, inline multi-select checklist, tag, or date-span editor beside the existing sort, pin, and hide actions. Keep filterValues controlled and filter the rows in the owner. Status-tag cells use the mood icon by default; override it only when a more specific icon improves recognition. Controls inside an active row remain independent, and opening a row context menu never activates or highlights that row. Column reorder and resize must offer the same outcome from pointer and keyboard, including pinned boundaries and cancellation. Pin only the few columns that remain essential while scrolling; the table limits effective pins by measured width so an unpinned reading area always remains reachable. Use categorical severity for named levels and numeric score only for the 0–10 severity scale; preserve other scales and units as truthful text. If the row needs a story, it probably is not a table row.
guidance.cx-table-view:
Use a table view when a filter bar, table, pagination, and bulk action bar belong to one coordinated collection. Define each filter once on CxTableColumn.filter and pass one controlled filterValues map; the filter button and matching column header use the same editor and stay synchronized. Only one filter surface remains open at a time.

The owner applies filtering, sorting, grouping, and pagination to collection or view state, then passes the resulting rows back. Quick-filter selection must never write the entities those rows represent. Supply a coherent set of relevant display, grouping, sorting, visibility, and pinning controls when using the built-in Table properties surface; if only one isolated property or a small subset of the collection pattern is useful, compose the smaller components instead.
guidance.cx-tabs:
Use tabs to switch between sibling views at the same level. Tabs should keep the user in place while changing the content below. Set controlsId when the tabs control a tab panel so the relationship is exposed semantically.

The neutral divider is present by default. Set divided to false when the surrounding surface already provides a clear boundary; this never removes the active-tab indicator. Keep labels short and stable. If there are too many tabs to scan, use overflow behavior rather than squeezing every label into view.
guidance.cx-tag:
Use a tag for compact metadata, categories, or applied filters. It should add context without becoming the main content. With a precise pointer, a dismissible tag stays quiet at rest and reveals its dismiss control in a reserved trailing lane on hover or keyboard focus, so it never covers the label. On touch, where hover does not exist, the dismiss control stays visible, in flow, and at least 24px square.

Make a tag interactive only when pressing it opens something scoped to that tag, such as the filter it represents. An interactive tag earns pointer and focus affordance the passive tag must never show, and its dismiss control stays a separate action beside it rather than inside it. Never make a tag interactive inside another button, a label, or a clickable row, where it would nest or steal the outer control's activation.

Do not use tags as decorations. Each tag should help the user understand or act.
guidance.cx-tag-field:
Use tag field when the user needs to search and manage multiple short values in one text-field surface. The focused inline input owns the combobox interaction while selected tags stay beside it; typing filters available tags, Up and Down move through suggestions, Enter toggles the active tag, and Space does the same when the query is empty. Escape closes the suggestions without discarding the query. With an empty input, Left or Backspace moves to the last selected tag; Backspace or Delete then removes it. Clear and pointer removal return focus to the inline input so selection can continue.

Leave creatable on when users may add missing tags. Create stays as the final popover option, Mod+Enter opens it directly, a typed query prefills the tag name, Cancel returns to the same query, and a created tag is selected immediately. Set creatable to false for selection-only uses such as table filters; selection, search, removal, and clear remain available while every create path is removed. Use a Select [thing] placeholder such as Select tags or Select recipients. Do not use tag field for a single choice or for long free-form content.
guidance.cx-steps:
Use steps when a process has a known sequence. Pass the exact sequence being presented and address the current position in that same array; derive conditional steps before they reach the component. The indicator is passive and is never disabled.

Use status pending only for an exceptional wait such as external processing, review, or required input. Pending replaces the numbered marker with an exclamation icon and updates the accessible status without changing the indexed position; it remains pending instead of becoming completed if the process advances. Add mood danger only when that wait needs attention; keep the explanation and recovery action outside the indicator. Compact density hides non-current labels without changing marker or connector size, while fill layout lets neutral connectors absorb the available width. Every step name and status remains available to assistive technology.
guidance.cx-text-area:
Use a text area for longer free text such as notes, descriptions, and comments. It gives the user room to think and revise.

Do not use placeholders. Put prompts, examples, and constraints in hint text. The visible hint or validation message must remain associated with the native textarea; validation replaces the hint, and only an error marks the field invalid. Do not use it for short values that should stay scannable in a form. A text field is cleaner for those.
guidance.cx-time-field:
Use time field when the user needs a specific time. Each hour or minute segment behaves as one editable unit: typing replaces that segment, complete values advance naturally, and one-digit values zero-pad when committed. Users can move with Tab, Left, Right, or a colon; adjust with Up and Down; and paste familiar forms such as 9, 930, 13:00, or 9:30 PM.

Use minuteStep for a real minute grid and min or max for allowed bounds. Impossible or out-of-range values stay visible with local recovery instead of silently changing or disappearing. Pair the field with a date when the day matters, and add a hint only when format or limits are not already clear from context.
guidance.cx-toast:
Use a toast for short feedback after an action. It should confirm, warn, or explain something lightweight without interrupting the user. Plain non-dismissible information may close after five seconds and must pause its remaining lifetime while hovered or focused.

Any visible action makes the toast persistent and dismissible; actionable notifications never auto-dismiss, and pressing an action does not close them implicitly. Explicitly dismissible toasts also persist. Do not use toasts for critical information or anything the user must read later. Important messages need a persistent place.
guidance.cx-toggle-button:
Use a toggle button for an action that can stay on or off, especially in toolbars. Off uses a quiet button surface; on uses a raised emphasis surface, so the pressed state remains obvious in every theme. Keep its accessible name stable when the icon changes with state.

Provide text or a base icon. Do not use it for navigation. If the user is switching views, tabs are clearer.
guidance.cx-toggle-chip:
Use a toggle chip for compact filter choices that can be turned on or off. It works well when several chips can sit together.

Keep chip labels short. If the choice needs explanation, use a larger control.
guidance.cx-toggle-chip-group:
Use a toggle chip group for a set of compact filters or modes. It should help users scan available choices and see what is active.

Do not use it for high-stakes choices. Chips are lightweight by nature.
guidance.cx-tooltip:
Use cxTooltip for brief optional clarification attached to an icon, label, control, or intentionally clipped value. Direct attachment to the real trigger is preferred; use the cx-tooltip composition wrapper when projection is the clearer fit. Both routes use the same shared surface, timing, placement, and accessibility behavior.

Never use the native HTML title attribute or a one-off tooltip implementation for user-facing help. For ordinary clarification, cxTooltip or text supplies the message. For clipped text, enable overflow mode and mark every independently clipped text target with data-cx-tooltip-overflow. One trigger measures all of its marked targets but opens only one shared surface: pointer hover reveals the clipped target under the pointer, while keyboard focus summarizes all clipped targets. A marked target's complete DOM text supplies its overflow message even when the base message is empty; use data-cx-tooltip-text only when an explicit accessible override is necessary. When there are no marked descendants, the host itself is measured and its complete DOM text supplies the message when the base message is empty. A passive overflow preview may only duplicate complete DOM text and must never contain essential instructions, state, consequences, recovery, or actions. Keep task-critical content visible outside the tooltip.
guidance.cx-tooltip-trigger:
Attach cxTooltip directly to the real button, link, field, or passive text renderer that needs brief optional clarification. This is the preferred trigger API for the shared cx-tooltip surface because it preserves the owner's layout and places aria-describedby on the native focus owner.

Use cxTooltipOverflow only for useful clipped-text previews. Mark every independently clipped descendant with data-cx-tooltip-overflow; the one directive measures them through the shared observer and owns one surface for the whole trigger. Pointer hover reveals the marked clipped target under the pointer, while keyboard focus summarizes all clipped targets. A marked target's complete DOM text supplies its overflow message even when cxTooltip is empty; use data-cx-tooltip-text only when that DOM text is not the right message. When no descendant is marked, the host itself is measured and its complete DOM text supplies the message when cxTooltip is empty. Never add tabindex to passive table cells, never use an HTML title attribute, and never build a separate tooltip surface.
guidance.cx-tree-view:
Use a tree view for nested structures where the user needs to expand, collapse, and understand hierarchy. It is useful for folders, scopes, and grouped navigation.

Keep the tree readable. If the hierarchy is too deep, add search or a simpler way to jump.
guidance.cx-trend-tag:
Use a trend tag to show direction or change in a compact way. It works best beside a metric or list item where the comparison matters.

Make the baseline clear. A trend without context can look meaningful while saying very little.
guidance.cx-utility-bar:
Utility bars are internal-only product chrome. Use one only for a clearly identified internal purpose, such as prototype controls, an admin bar, or operator tooling.

Never use a utility bar in a public-facing interface or expose one to ordinary users.
guidance.cx-wizard-dialog:
Use a wizard dialog for a genuinely sequential task whose later decisions depend on earlier ones. Pass the exact step sequence currently presented and keep index in that sequence. When a choice changes the branch, the owner derives the new array and explicitly remaps the current step by id; the dialog never searches hidden steps or chooses a replacement. If that change removes the control that held focus, including step-specific sidebar content, the wizard moves focus after render to the destination step's established heading or first meaningful control. It preserves focus on persistent controls and does not steal it for unrelated background changes, so consumers never add step-specific focus targets, document listeners, or timers.

Only the topmost visible, active overlay owns Escape. While the wizard is eligible, Escape follows the same Cancel or Back path as the visible secondary button; a nested child overlay consumes it first, and a loading wizard still blocks the key from every surface behind it without changing step. After close teardown and surviving-parent focus maintenance settle, the exact connected, visible, and focusable invoker is the final focus target unless a newer top overlay opened. An invalid invoker falls back to the established target inside its owning surviving parent surface.

Let Back preserve compatible work, make the final outcome explicit, and keep every visually suppressed step label available as an accessible name.
